citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X,Y,Z$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over one scalar field, let $F:X\to Y$ and $G:Y\to Z$ be compact linear maps, and set $A:=G\circ F:X\to Z$. For spectral regularization families $R^G_\alpha:Z\to Y$ for $G^\dagger$ and $R^F_\gamma:Y\to X$ for $F^\dagger$, and a parameter rule $(\alpha,\gamma):(0,\infty)\times Z\to(0,\infty)^2$, define $T_\delta(z^\delta):=R^F_{\gamma(\delta,z^\delta)}(R^G_{\alpha(\delta,z^\delta)}z^\delta)$ for $z^\delta\in Z$. The order is fixed by the factorization: first regularize $G$, then $F$; no general identity $A^\dagger=F^\dagger G^\dagger$ is part of this definition.

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator. The associated compact linear inverse
model has parameter space $X$, data space $Y$, forward map $K$, and admissible
truth class $X$: for a true parameter $x^\dagger\in X$, the exact datum is
$y=Kx^\dagger\in Y$. Given an exact datum $y\in Y$, solving this inverse
problem means finding a parameter $x\in X$ such that $Kx=y$. No injectivity,
surjectivity, or closed-range assumption is included in the model.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex Hilbert
spaces over the same scalar field, and let $K:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear
operator. Write $R(K):=\{Kx:x\in X\}$ for its range,
$N(K):=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ for its kernel, and
$M^\perp:=\{z:\langle z,m\rangle=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$ for the
orthogonal complement of a subspace $M$. The kernel $N(K)$ is closed, so the
restriction
$$\widetilde K:=K|_{N(K)^\perp}:N(K)^\perp\to R(K)$$
is a linear bijection. Define the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger$
to have domain
$$D(K^\dagger):=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp$$
and, for the unique decomposition $y=r+z$ with $r\in R(K)$ and
$z\in R(K)^\perp$, set
$$K^\dagger y:=\widetilde K^{-1}r.$$
Thus $K^\dagger y$ is the unique minimum-norm solution of $Kx=r$, and the
orthogonal-range component is mapped to zero. Boundedness of $K^\dagger$ on
this domain is not part of the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]), let $|T|$ and the singular values $s_n(T)$ be
as in the absolute-value definition
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Let
$J=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$ when $\operatorname{ran}T$ is infinite-dimensional. When
$\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite-dimensional, put
$r:=\dim\operatorname{ran}T\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-dimension]]) and let
$J=\{1,\dots,r\}$, interpreted as $\varnothing$ when $r=0$. Thus $J$ indexes
exactly the positive singular values counted with multiplicity, which we write
as $(s_j)_{j\in J}$ in nonincreasing order. Then:

1. there are orthonormal families $(e_j)_{j\in J}$ in $(\ker T)^\perp$ and
   $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ in $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$, indexed by exactly $J$,
   with $|T|e_j=s_je_j$ and $f_j=s_j^{-1}Te_j$ for every $j\in J$;
2. for every $x\in H$ the series converges in norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle x,e_j\rangle f_j,$$
   and its finite partial sums
   $T_n:=\sum_{j\le n}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ satisfy
   $\|T-T_n\|\le s_{n+1}$ for every $n$ with $n+1\in J$ (and $T_n=T$ for
   $n\ge r$ when $r<+\infty$);
3. the linear map $U$ defined on the span of $\{e_j:j\in J\}$ by $Ue_j:=f_j$,
   extended by continuity to $(\ker T)^\perp$ and by zero on $\ker T$, is a
   **partial isometry** with
   $$T=U|T|,\qquad U^*U=P_{(\ker T)^\perp},\qquad U^*U\text{ is the orthogonal projection onto }(\ker T)^\perp,$$
   and $UU^*$ the orthogonal projection onto $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$;
4. the zero-padded sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ is *not* used to index the
   orthonormal systems: the systems carry exactly the index set $J$ of the
   positive singular values, and the terms $s_n(T)=0$ beyond the rank in the
   finite-rank case are numerical padding only.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact and bounded. Put $S=A^*A$. By
[[lem-compact-gram-operator-is-positive-and-has-kernel]], $S$ is compact,
positive, and self-adjoint, with $\ker S=\ker A$. Let $\Sigma$ be the set of
nonzero eigenvalues of $S$ and $P_t$ the orthogonal projection onto the
eigenspace of $t\in\Sigma$; let $P_0$ be the orthogonal projection onto
$\ker S$. The compact spectral multiplier of a bounded scalar function
$q:\{0\}\cup\Sigma\to\mathbb F$ is
$$q(S)x:=q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in\Sigma}q(t)P_tx,$$
where the finite-subset net converges in norm by
[[lem-compact-spectral-multiplier-is-well-defined]]. For $\nu>0$, define
$S^\nu$ by the multiplier $q_\nu(0)=0$ and $q_\nu(t)=t^\nu$ for $t>0$.
This multiplier is bounded: if $t\in\Sigma$ and $u\in E_t$ is a unit vector,
then $0<t=\|Su\|\le\|S\|$, so $|q_\nu(t)|\le\|S\|^\nu$.

For $\lambda>0$, the Tikhonov filter and residual filter are
$$g_\lambda(t)=\frac1{t+\lambda},\qquad r_\lambda(t)=1-tg_\lambda(t)=\frac{\lambda}{t+\lambda}.$$
The Tikhonov solution for data $y_\delta\in Y$ is
$$x_\lambda^\delta=g_\lambda(S)A^*y_\delta =(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*y_\delta.$$
Indeed, the spectral decomposition gives $S+\lambda I_X$ the multiplier
$t+\lambda$ on each $E_t$ and $\lambda$ on $\ker S$, so $g_\lambda(S)$ is
its inverse, whose existence is also supplied by
[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]].
The source condition of order $\nu>0$ and radius $R\ge0$ means that
$x^\dagger=S^\nu w$ for some $w\in X$ with $\|w\|\le R$. A family of
filters $g_\alpha$ with residual filters $r_\alpha(t)=1-tg_\alpha(t)$ has
qualification at least $p>0$ when, for each $0<\nu\le p$, some finite
constant $C_\nu\ge0$ satisfies
$$t^\nu|r_\alpha(t)|\le C_\nu\alpha^\nu \quad\text{for every }\alpha>0\text{ and }t\in\Sigma.$$
When $\Sigma=\varnothing$, this condition is vacuous.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
Rectangular matrix multiplication and the identity matrix $I_n$, including zero-sized shapes and
In orthonormal bases, the matrix of the adjoint is the conjugate transpose of the matrix.

For every matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or
$\mathbb C$, there exists a unique matrix $A^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$
satisfying the four Penrose equations of
The Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse $A^+$ as the solution of the four Penrose equations.

derivations.claim: Since $G^*G=\operatorname{diag}(9,16)$ and $F^*F=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)$, the specified Tikhonov maps are $R^G_\alpha=\operatorname{diag}(3/(9+\alpha),4/(16+\alpha))$ and $R^F_\gamma=\operatorname{diag}(2/(4+\gamma),1/(1+\gamma))$.
Multiplying in the required order gives $A=\operatorname{diag}(6,4)$ and $R^F_\gamma R^G_\alpha z=\operatorname{diag}(6/((4+\gamma)(9+\alpha)),4/((1+\gamma)(16+\alpha)))z$.

As $\alpha,\gamma\downarrow0$, the diagonal coefficients tend to $1/6$ and $1/4$, so the estimate tends to $A^{-1}z$ for $A=\operatorname{diag}(6,4)$. Since $AA^{-1}=I=A^{-1}A$, we have $AA^{-1}A=A$, $A^{-1}AA^{-1}=A^{-1}$, and both square products are the self-adjoint identity; [F3]–[F4] therefore give $A^+=A^{-1}$. The same argument gives $F^+=F^{-1}$ and $G^+=G^{-1}$, and $F^{-1}G^{-1}=(GF)^{-1}=A^{-1}$.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $FG=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $GF=A=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, which are unequal. Each of $F,G,A$ is nonzero with a one-dimensional image, so both factors are rank deficient and noncommuting.

Put $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Multiplication gives $AB=G$ and $BA=F$. Since $F$ and $G$ are self-adjoint idempotents, $ABA=(AB)A=GA=G^2F=A$, $BAB=(BA)B=FB=B$, and both $AB$ and $BA$ are self-adjoint. Thus $B$ satisfies all four equations in [F2], so $A^+=B$ by [F3].

The same equations show $F^+=F$ and $G^+=G$, because each is a self-adjoint idempotent and hence satisfies the four Penrose equations; uniqueness in [F3] identifies them. Therefore $F^+G^+=FG=\frac12B\ne B=A^+$. This refutes the universal identity.
